title: Windigo
summary: Windigo is a cybercrime operation that public reporting describes as compromising large numbers of Linux servers, particularly shared hosting, content management and mail systems, to redirect visitors and deliver malicious content. Research published from around 2014 onward linked the operation to the Ebury credential-stealing rootkit and to Cdorked, a backdoor used on web servers to alter the pages they served. The campaign is notable for scale rather than stealth, because one compromised server could silently redirect traffic for hundreds of hosted websites and their visitors. Analysts observed that the Ebury family persisted in hosting environments for years and appeared in later intrusions, even after the main wave of activity was reported to have declined. Evidence includes altered server binaries, unexpected SSH (Secure Shell) keys or password captures, changed web server configuration and redirect rules added to hosted sites.

beginner.definition: Windigo is the name for a criminal operation that took over many web servers at once. It mostly attacked Linux servers, which are common in web hosting. It changed the websites those servers hosted, so visitors were sent to harmful pages. The tools it used are called Ebury and Cdorked.
beginner.whyItMatters: One broken server can send thousands of visitors to a malicious page. That spreads malware to people who trusted the website. If your company rents hosting and never checks the server, you may spread harm without knowing it. This case also shows that Linux servers need the same care as Windows laptops, because attackers do not ignore them.
howItWorks: The attackers break into a hosting server, often by using stolen Secure Shell logins or known software weaknesses.
They install a rootkit, which is software that hides itself and other tools from the system.
A second tool, a backdoor, changes the pages the server sends to visitors.
Visitors see a normal website, but some of them are redirected to harmful content.
The attackers copy login details from the server so they can keep returning.
Because many websites share one server, a single break-in affects all of them.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk that also handles the post. Someone swaps the labels on the out tray, so letters go to the wrong building. Patients still trust the desk, and the letters look normal. Nobody notices, because the desk itself works fine. Windigo swapped labels on web servers in the same way. The websites looked normal, but some visitors were quietly sent somewhere dangerous.
takeaways: Linux and shared hosting servers need patching, monitoring and key reviews.
A redirect added to a website can be a sign that the server itself is compromised.
Stolen Secure Shell keys let an attacker return long after the first clean-up.

objectives: Explain what Windigo is and why it focused on Linux hosting servers.
Describe the roles of the Ebury and Cdorked tools in the operation.
Explain how one compromised server affects many websites and their visitors.
Recognise evidence such as altered binaries, new Secure Shell keys and redirect rules.
Summarise why server-side rootkits are hard to remove once installed.
Relate this case to the everyday need for patching and access reviews on servers.
